CHAPTER 1.1 · LEARNING AREA 1 · AUGUST · SEPTEMBER

Conditional probability

A medical test is positive. How certain is the disease? People who come by bus are late more often. Is that chance? As soon as you know something, probabilities change. In this chapter you calculate with this knowledge and check when two events really have nothing to do with each other.

8 LESSONS2 UNITSFOLLOWS ON FROM YEAR 11
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • determine conditional probabilities $P_B(A)$ from tree diagrams and two-way tables
  • reverse trees: from $P_A(B)$ to $P_B(A)$
  • check stochastic independence and tell it apart from mutual exclusivity
  • interpret results in context, for example in medical tests

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Probability under a condition

At a school, 250 students were asked: do you come by bus ($B$)? Were you late this week ($L$)?

$L$$\overline{L}$Total
$B$30120150
$\overline{B}$1090100
Total40210250

Altogether $\tfrac{40}{250} = 16\%$ were late. If you look only at the bus riders, it is $\tfrac{30}{150} = 20\%$, among the others only $\tfrac{10}{100} = 10\%$. The condition “comes by bus” shrinks the population to 150 people.

KEY POINT · CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY

The probability of $A$ given $B$ (with $P(B) > 0$) is $$P_B(A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}.$$

Rearranged, this gives the multiplication rule $P(A \cap B) = P(B) \cdot P_B(A)$. In a tree diagram, exactly these conditional probabilities are on the second stage.

Careful: $P_B(A)$ and $P_A(B)$ are in general different.

Notation: instead of $P_B(A)$ you will also find $P(A \mid B)$, read “P of A given B”.

Reversed tree: from one two-way table you can draw two trees, one with $B$ first and one with $L$ first. Both describe the same four probabilities of the intersections.

INTERACTIVE · THE RAPID TEST

Set how common the disease is and how well the test works. Watch how many of those who test positive are really ill.

EXAMPLE 1 · BUS AND BEING LATE

Use the table above to find $P_B(L)$ and $P_L(B)$. Interpret both numbers.

$P_B(L) = \tfrac{30}{150} = 0.2$: of the bus riders, 20% were late.

$P_L(B) = \tfrac{30}{40} = 0.75$: of those who were late, 75% came by bus. Two different questions, two different answers.

EXAMPLE 2 · THE POSITIVE TEST

2% are ill ($D$). The test detects 90% of the ill and is wrongly positive in 5% of the healthy. What is $P_+(D)$?

$P(D \cap +) = 0.02 \cdot 0.9 = 0.018$ and $P(\overline{D} \cap +) = 0.98 \cdot 0.05 = 0.049$, so $P(+) = 0.067$.

$P_+(D) = \dfrac{0.018}{0.067} \approx 0.269$. Only just over one in four people with a positive test is ill. The reason: there are many more healthy people than ill ones.

EXERCISES

Of 300 people asked, 120 wear glasses ($G$). 45 people with glasses and 54 people without glasses read every day ($R$). Draw up the two-way table and calculate $P(R)$, $P_G(R)$ and $P_R(G)$.

$G$: 45 | 75 | 120 · $\overline{G}$: 54 | 126 | 180 · Total: 99 | 201 | 300.

$P(R) = \tfrac{99}{300} = 0.33$, $P_G(R) = \tfrac{45}{120} = 0.375$, $P_R(G) = \tfrac{45}{99} \approx 0.455$

In the tree, $P(A) = 0.6$, $P_A(B) = 0.3$ and $P_{\overline{A}}(B) = 0.5$. Calculate $P(B)$ and $P_B(A)$.

$P(B) = 0.6 \cdot 0.3 + 0.4 \cdot 0.5 = 0.18 + 0.2 = 0.38$, $P_B(A) = \tfrac{0.18}{0.38} \approx 0.474$

Machine M1 makes 70% of all parts, 2% of them are faulty. Machine M2 makes 30%, 5% of them are faulty. A part is faulty. What is the probability that it comes from M2?

$P(F) = 0.7 \cdot 0.02 + 0.3 \cdot 0.05 = 0.014 + 0.015 = 0.029$, $P_F(M_2) = \tfrac{0.015}{0.029} \approx 0.517$. Although M2 makes fewer parts, more than half of the faulty parts come from there.

You are given $P(A) = 0.4$, $P_A(B) = 0.25$ and $P(B) = 0.3$. Complete the two-way table and draw the reversed tree ($B$ first). What are $P_B(A)$ and $P_{\overline{B}}(A)$?

$P(A \cap B) = 0.1$, $P(A \cap \overline{B}) = 0.3$, $P(\overline{A} \cap B) = 0.2$, $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 0.4$.

$P_B(A) = \tfrac{0.1}{0.3} = \tfrac13$, $P_{\overline{B}}(A) = \tfrac{0.3}{0.7} \approx 0.429$

According to example 2, someone with a positive test is only ill with a probability of about 26.9%. The person takes a second, independent test of the same kind, which is positive again. How likely is it now that the person is ill?

Take 0.269 as the new starting probability for $D$ and calculate as in example 2.

$\dfrac{0.269 \cdot 0.9}{0.269 \cdot 0.9 + 0.731 \cdot 0.05} = \dfrac{0.2421}{0.2421 + 0.03655} \approx 0.869$. After two positive tests about 87%. That is why a positive rapid test is usually confirmed by a second test.

Of 50 people, 20 have a dog. 12 of the dog owners go jogging every day. What is the probability that a dog owner goes jogging every day?

$\tfrac{12}{20} = 0.6$

$P(A) = 0.5$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. What is $P_A(B)$?

$\tfrac{0.2}{0.5} = 0.4$

$P(A) = 0.3$, $P_A(B) = 0.5$, $P_{\overline{A}}(B) = 0.2$. What is $P(B)$?

$0.3 \cdot 0.5 + 0.7 \cdot 0.2 = 0.15 + 0.14 = 0.29$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Stochastic independence

A dice is rolled. $A$: an even number. $B$: at most 2. Does the chance of an even number change if you know that at most 2 was rolled?

$P(A) = \tfrac12$. Given $B = \{1, 2\}$, only the 2 is even, so $P_B(A) = \tfrac12$. Knowing about $B$ changes nothing about $A$. Such events are called independent. With bus and being late it was different: $P_B(L) = 0.2$, but $P(L) = 0.16$.

KEY POINT · INDEPENDENCE

Two events $A$ and $B$ are called stochastically independent if $$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B).$$

For $P(B) > 0$ this is equivalent to $P_B(A) = P(A)$. Otherwise $A$ and $B$ are called dependent.

Mutually exclusive means something else: $A \cap B = \emptyset$, the events cannot happen together. Mutually exclusive events with $P(A) > 0$ and $P(B) > 0$ are always dependent.

In the tree: $A$ and $B$ are independent if both branches of the second stage carry the same probability for $B$: $P_A(B) = P_{\overline{A}}(B)$.

Dependent does not mean causal: dependence shows a connection, but not what the cause is.

INTERACTIVE · INDEPENDENT OR NOT?

Change $P(A)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A \cap B)$. In the unit square the left column is $B$, the right one $\overline{B}$. Gold is the share of $A$ in each.

EXAMPLE 3 · BUS AND BEING LATE

Are $B$ (bus) and $L$ (late) from unit 1 independent?

$P(B) \cdot P(L) = 0.6 \cdot 0.16 = 0.096$, but $P(B \cap L) = \tfrac{30}{250} = 0.12$. Dependent.

EXAMPLE 4 · A TOTAL OF 7

Two dice. $A$: the first shows a six. $B$: the total score is 7. Independent?

$P(A) = \tfrac16$, $P(B) = \tfrac{6}{36} = \tfrac16$, $P(A \cap B) = P(\{(6, 1)\}) = \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac16$. Independent. Whatever the first dice shows: exactly one number on the second makes it up to 7.

THE DICE GAMETree diagrams and path rules

EXERCISES

$P(A) = 0.4$ and $P(B) = 0.5$. Are $A$ and $B$ independent if a) $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$   b) $P(A \cap B) = 0.25$?

$P(A) \cdot P(B) = 0.2$. a) independent   b) dependent

One dice: $A$ = “1”, $B$ = “6”. Are the events mutually exclusive? Are they independent?

Mutually exclusive, because both at once is impossible. $P(A \cap B) = 0 \neq \tfrac16 \cdot \tfrac16$, so dependent: if you know that a 6 was rolled, you know for sure that no 1 was rolled.

$A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.3$ and $P(B) = 0.6$. Complete the two-way table with probabilities.

$P(A \cap B) = 0.18$, $P(A \cap \overline{B}) = 0.12$, $P(\overline{A} \cap B) = 0.42$, $P(\overline{A} \cap \overline{B}) = 0.28$. Every cell is the product of its marginal values.

Two dice: $A$ = “total score 8”, $B$ = “first dice shows 6”. Check for independence and compare with example 4.

$P(A) = \tfrac{5}{36}$, $P(B) = \tfrac16$, $P(A \cap B) = P(\{(6, 2)\}) = \tfrac{1}{36} = \tfrac{6}{216}$, but $P(A) \cdot P(B) = \tfrac{5}{216}$. Dependent: with a 1 on the first roll a total of 8 is impossible, with a 6 it is not.

Two pumps fail independently of each other, each with a probability of 5%. How likely is a failure of the system if a) one pump is enough, b) both have to run? Why is the assumption of independence questionable here?

a) both fail: $0.05^2 = 0.0025$   b) at least one fails: $1 - 0.95^2 = 0.0975$.

A common cause (power cut, flood) often stops both at the same time. Then the failures are dependent and a) is far too optimistic.

$0.5 \cdot 0.4 = 0.2$

$P(A) = 0.2$, $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. Then $A$ and $B$ are …

$0.2 \cdot 0.3 = 0.06 \neq 0.1$

$A$ and $B$ are independent with $P(A) = 0.25$ and $P(B) = 0.8$. What is $P(A \cap \overline{B})$?

$A$ and $\overline{B}$ are independent too: $0.25 \cdot 0.2 = 0.05$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT
TRAINING · COMPLETING TWO-WAY TABLES

In a year group of 120 students, 48 take computer science ($C$), 30 of them are also in the drama club ($T$). Altogether 50 are in the drama club. Calculate $P_C(T)$ and $P_T(C)$. Are $C$ and $T$ independent?

$P_C(T) = \tfrac{30}{48} = 0.625$, $P_T(C) = \tfrac{30}{50} = 0.6$. $P(C) \cdot P(T) = 0.4 \cdot \tfrac{5}{12} \approx 0.167$, but $P(C \cap T) = 0.25$: dependent.

40% of all emails are spam. The word “prize” appears in 30% of spam emails, but only in 2% of the others. An email contains “prize”. How likely is it to be spam?

$\dfrac{0.4 \cdot 0.3}{0.4 \cdot 0.3 + 0.6 \cdot 0.02} = \dfrac{0.12}{0.132} \approx 0.909$. This is how simple spam filters work.

Connecting with Year 11: in the Monty Hall problem you choose door 1, the host opens door 3 with a goat. Use conditional probabilities to explain why switching wins with $\tfrac23$.

If the car is behind door 2 (probability $\tfrac13$), the host has to open door 3. If it is behind door 1 ($\tfrac13$), he opens door 3 only with $\tfrac12$. $P_{\text{opens 3}}(\text{car behind 2}) = \dfrac{\frac13 \cdot 1}{\frac13 \cdot 1 + \frac13 \cdot \frac12} = \tfrac23$.

Prove: if $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $A$ and $\overline{B}$ are independent too.

$P(A \cap \overline{B}) = P(A) - P(A \cap B) = P(A) - P(A) \cdot P(B) = P(A) \cdot (1 - P(B)) = P(A) \cdot P(\overline{B})$.

EXCURSIONWHEN INDEPENDENCE IS WRONGLY ASSUMED

The Sally Clark case

In 1999 the solicitor Sally Clark was convicted in England because her two sons had died shortly after birth. A paediatrician testified as an expert witness that in a family like hers the probability of a sudden infant death was about 1 in 8,543. For two cases he multiplied: $\left(\tfrac{1}{8543}\right)^2 \approx \tfrac{1}{73{,}000{,}000}$.

Multiplying assumes that the two deaths are independent. Shared genetic or domestic causes, however, make a second case much more likely. There was a second mistake as well: even a small probability of the data under the assumption of innocence is not the probability of innocence. $P_{\text{innocent}}(\text{data})$ and $P_{\text{data}}(\text{innocent})$ are different things, like $P_B(L)$ and $P_L(B)$.

In 2001 the Royal Statistical Society publicly pointed out these mistakes. In 2003 the conviction was quashed.

Sources: Royal Statistical Society, statement on the Sally Clark case of 23 October 2001; Court of Appeal, R v Clark [2003] EWCA Crim 1020.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

CONDITIONAL PROBABILITY

$P_B(A) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, the population shrinks to $B$.

Bus: $P_B(L) = \tfrac{30}{150} = 0.2$ · $P_L(B) = \tfrac{30}{40} = 0.75$

MULTIPLICATION RULE AND TREE

$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P_A(B)$. Second stage of the tree: conditional probabilities.

Reversed tree from the same two-way table

INDEPENDENCE

$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$, equivalent to $P_B(A) = P(A)$.

First dice 6 and total score 7: independent

MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE ≠ INDEPENDENT

$A \cap B = \emptyset$. With positive probabilities always dependent.

“1” and “6” with one dice

INTERPRETING

Positive tests for rare diseases are often false positives.

2% ill, 90% / 5%: $P_+(D) \approx 27\%$
